extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters learning police/crime reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for reporting police beats and crime stories: how to open, structure, and furnish a police/crime news item with necessary facts, human detail, procedural context, and social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic narrative lead / in medias res openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Open crime stories with an immediate, vivid scene or action to draw readers in (examples on this page begin in the middle of a fight or chase: “Beat him up,” yelled the gang; a man runs with a shotgun behind him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start in the action—use short, active sentences and sensory verbs to establish urgency and set the scene (e.g., fights, shots fired, running). The page demonstrates multiple incident openings that thrust the reader directly into events rather than beginning with abstract summarization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific identifying facts (names, addresses, ages, occupations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete identifiers for victims, suspects, and principals (e.g., “Walter H. Hammond… head of the Hammond and Wilson Stock Company… lived at No. 314 Harrison avenue,” or ages like “a boy of 19”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full names, occupations, exact addresses and ages where available to give the story credibility and allow readers to place people geographically and socially; include organizational affiliations (banks, clubs) when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct speech and eyewitness dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Include quoted speech from participants, bystanders, family members, and policemen (e.g., “‘I never knew that any of these conductors could fight,’ he sputtered…”, Mrs. Sheehan’s extended recollection of her son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy dialogue to convey personality, human reaction, and immediacy. Long, well-placed quotes can humanize victims and witnesses; short exclamations or commands dramatize the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police and procedural detail (arrests, stations, officers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the concrete procedural actions and actors—names/ranks of arresting officers, stations, cells, arrests made or prevented (e.g., “Police-men Wilson and Dempsey, of the Morrisania station…”, “led to a cell in the Morrisania station”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include where arrests were made, which station handled the case, and immediate law-enforcement moves. These details lend authority and allow readers to follow the case’s official trail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical/coroner findings and victims’ conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: State specific injuries, causes of death, and hospital condition (e.g., “The bullet entered the left temple and ploughed into the brain,” “ambulance surgeon found five thrusts,” “in a dangerous hysterical condition”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report precise medical findings when available; note hospital transfers, doctors’ assessments, and whether wounds were fatal or non-fatal. This clarifies the severity and factual basis of the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situating incidents within patterns or chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: Place single crimes in a broader pattern by listing similar recent incidents or compiling chronologies (example: listing murders in Little Italy since Jan. 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize an incident with related events or statistics to indicate whether it is isolated or part of a trend; use dates and short summaries to show recurrence and amplify significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reported facts from accusations/speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute claims and uncertain information to sources—police say, witnesses claim, it is said—rather than presenting unverified assertions as fact (e.g., “The police say…”, “It is said that Grew complained…”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label hearsay and accusations clearly; avoid authorial speculation about motive. This maintains accuracy and legal defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include social and institutional context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain structural or social factors that frame the incident (e.g., understaffing of patrolmen in Little Italy, neighborhood conditions, presence/absence of police beats).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relevant, provide statistics, official commentary, or social description that helps readers understand contributing conditions beyond the immediate event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest backstory and family reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Add personal history and family responses to deepen reader engagement (examples: Gene’s mother’s recollections, the runaway boy’s background, Mandy’s family situation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use biographical detail, quotes from relatives, and scenes of domestic reaction to make the story emotionally resonant and to explain the human stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise description of method and weapons
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the means of the crime, weapon types, wound locations and distinctive physical evidence (e.g., “stiletto… bent double,” “shotgun… one barrel,” bullets fired into body after fall).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about weapons and how they were used; such detail is important for clarity and for any follow-up reporting on charges or forensics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear chronological sequencing of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell what happened in order—approach, confrontation, action, immediate aftermath, pursuit/arrest (e.g., run, halt, the shot, then arrival of police).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out events step by step so readers can reconstruct the incident; use time markers (minutes, hours), locations, and transitional phrases to maintain clarity in complex incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report prior relationships, motives, and history when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Include background relationships and prior incidents that bear on motive or cause (e.g., Grew had been befriended by Hammond, previously threatened him; past arrests for selling oleomargarine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantiated, report prior disputes, threats, business ties, or criminal records that help explain why the incident may have occurred—attribute assertions to sources if not independently verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document legal/institutional outcomes and next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Note immediate legal status and likely proceedings: arraignment, commitment, held without bail, charges, jail sentences (examples throughout: arraigned before Judge Harmon, held without bail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell readers what will happen next from a legal standpoint and record official dispositions, bail status, and court actions to complete the factual arc of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete sensory and visual detail to convey scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ vivid images and sensory lists to convey the chaos or atmosphere (e.g., “Pieces of hats, feathers, ribbons and lingerie were scattered from end to end of the car”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scatter precise, evocative details to create a clear mental picture; such details also serve as evidence of the scene’s seriousness and help readers visualize events.
